messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 39
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Construction Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 73

He is thirty-nine now, a construction worker who has spent most of his adult life on job sites where noise, risk, and physical strain are ordinary parts of the day. He talks about work with a kind of plain pride. He knows how to read a site, how to move heavy materials safely, how to notice when something is off before anyone else does. For years, that ability made him feel steady. Then, about three years ago, he watches a coworker die.

It happens on an early morning shift at a commercial building project. They are behind schedule, and everyone is moving fast. He is guiding materials across an active area when he hears shouting, then the sharp metallic crash that still seems to live somewhere inside his body. A section of equipment fails. His coworker, a man he has worked beside for months, is struck and pinned before anyone can reach him. He remembers running toward the scene and then stopping short, feeling useless and horrified. He remembers the man’s face, the unnatural angle of his body, the sound of other workers yelling for help. He remembers the smell of dust and hydraulic fluid, and how bright the morning light seems against the concrete. By the time emergency responders arrive, he already knows his coworker is gone.

In the first days after, he tells himself he is lucky it was not him. He repeats this to other people and to himself as if saying it enough times will make the shaking stop. At home, he tries not to talk about what happened. His wife asks questions, but he shrugs her off, sits in silence, or goes outside to smoke. At night he closes his eyes and sees the scene again with a clarity that feels cruel. Sometimes the replay begins with the crash; sometimes it begins with the split second before, when everything still seems normal. He wakes drenched in sweat, heart hammering, already scanning the room before he fully knows where he is.

He returns to work sooner than he wants to because bills do not wait. On the site, he is changed. He startles violently at the slam of steel, the backfire of engines, the sudden drop of a tool. When machinery grinds or alarms sound, his chest tightens and his vision narrows. He finds himself watching everyone constantly, unable to focus on his own task because he is checking harnesses, loads, angles, distances. He tells himself he is just being careful, but coworkers begin to notice he is jumpy, irritable, and slower than before. He cannot walk past the part of the site where the accident happened without feeling a wave of nausea. Later, on other jobs, certain smells or sounds throw him right back there. For a few seconds he is no longer in the present; he is at that building again, hearing the crash.

At home, he becomes harder to reach. Before the accident, he is not a talkative man, but he jokes with his kids, grills on weekends, and takes satisfaction in ordinary routines. Afterward, he spends more time alone in the garage or sitting in his truck after work, delaying going inside. He feels ashamed of how easily anger comes now. Small things set him off—a spilled drink, the television too loud, a question asked twice. He sees fear and confusion on his children’s faces and hates himself for it. His marriage, already strained by long hours and money stress, begins to fray faster. His wife tells him he is distant, that even when he is home he seems somewhere else. He cannot explain that she is right.

He starts sleeping with the television on because silence makes room for the memories. He avoids the news when there are stories about workplace accidents. He takes different routes to avoid passing the building where it happened, even after the project is long finished. His world gets smaller without him fully noticing. Crowded hardware stores make him tense. Restaurants feel too loud. He chooses corners, watches exits, sits with his back to the wall. On bad days, his body feels like it is braced for impact from the moment he wakes up.

The divorce comes about a year and a half after the accident. He describes it without bitterness, mostly with exhaustion. He says his ex-wife got tired of “living around” his moods. Now he lives alone in a rented apartment and sees his kids on a schedule he keeps carefully, almost rigidly, because it is one of the few things he still trusts himself not to ruin. He continues to work, though every shift costs him. He is dependable and rarely calls out, but he lives in a state of constant internal strain. He scans for danger, replays what he should have done differently, and carries a private conviction that he failed the man who died.

When he talks about that morning now, his voice stays flat at first, but his hands give him away. They clench and unclench against his knees. He says he knows, rationally, that the equipment failure was not his fault. Yet he still believes he should have seen something, should have moved faster, should have done more. He does not feel like the same man he was before. The job that once made him feel capable now keeps him in daily contact with the kind of sounds, smells, and sudden risks that his body no longer knows how to file away as ordinary. He keeps going to work, keeps showing up for his children, keeps trying to outrun a moment that returns uninvited, again and again, as if it is still happening.
